hero.title: Apple
hero.desc: Founded April 1, 1976 on Crist Drive in Los Altos by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Forty-nine years later the same company sells nearly a billion handheld computers a year and is, by market value, the largest single business in human history.

spotlight.title: iPhone
spotlight.desc: The handheld computer that redefined consumer electronics. Launched in 2007 — 18 years and 3 billion units later, Apple's most defining product and the largest single-revenue product line in human history.

overview.heading: A company built on the bitten apple, the bezier curve, and the relentless deletion of anything that doesn't ship.
paragraphs: Apple Inc. is an American technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs and sells consumer electronics, computer software, online services, and — since 2020 — its own silicon. The company is structured around vertical integration across hardware, software, and services, a model Steve Jobs called "the whole widget."

Apple's history splits cleanly into five eras. The founding period (1976–1985) produced the Apple I, II, and the original 1984 Macintosh. The wilderness years (1985–1997) saw three CEOs and a billion-dollar loss. The restoration (1997–2007) brought the iMac, OS X, and the iPod. The iPhone era (2007–2011) reshaped consumer electronics globally. The Cook era (2011–present) made Apple the first company to cross $1T, $2T, and $3T in market capitalisation.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (2nd generation)
hero.desc: The second iPod touch fixed the most glaring omission of the first: it arrived with a built-in speaker. Redesigned with a rounded stainless back that echoed the iPhone 3G, it also added Nike+ wireless support without an adapter, external volume buttons, and a flush headphone jack. The same 3.5-inch display. Faster internals. A shape refined enough to last as the template for the next several generations.

overview.heading: The first iPod touch that felt finished.
paragraphs: The original iPod touch launched in 2007 as a screen-first proposition — a pocket-sized multi-touch display for music, the web, and eventually apps. It was remarkable hardware for its moment, but it shipped with one obvious gap: no speaker. Listening required headphones, always. The second generation closed that gap, and in doing so made the device feel categorically more useful.

Announced on September 9, 2008 at Apple's "Let's Rock" music-focused media event, the second-generation touch debuted alongside updated iPod nano and iPod classic models. It shipped the same day at $229 (8 GB), $299 (16 GB), and $399 (32 GB). The price positioned it squarely as a premium music device — not a phone, but closer to the total iPhone experience than anything else Apple made.

The redesign was substantial. The flat aluminum back of the first generation gave way to a polished stainless steel curved back that matched the iPhone 3G's aesthetic. The device became 30% thinner — 8.5 mm at its thickest, tapering toward the edges — and lighter at 115 grams. External volume buttons appeared on the left edge for the first time, the headphone jack was recessed flush with the casing, and the internal speaker sat behind a small grille at the top of the back panel.

Nike+ wireless support arrived without any external adapter. Where the original required a small receiver plugged into the dock connector to communicate with Nike+ sensor-equipped shoes, the second generation handled it natively over a built-in wireless module. For runners already in the Nike+ ecosystem, this alone was a meaningful upgrade.

Internally, the device carried a Samsung-manufactured ARM processor running at 533 MHz — faster than its predecessor — paired with 128 MB of RAM. It launched running iPhone OS 2.1 with full App Store access, a category the original touch received only via a $9.95 paid software update in 2008. The second generation had it from day one.

Software support extended through iOS 4.2.1, released in November 2010 — a notably extended lifespan for a device discontinued in June of that year. After discontinuation, the third generation (September 2009) continued with the same external design, differing primarily in processor speed. The second generation's form factor was, in effect, the template that defined the iPod touch's look for four years.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (3rd generation)
hero.desc: The third iPod touch wore the same face as the second but hid a fundamentally different machine inside. A new processor, doubled RAM, and a gaming-grade GPU transformed it from a music player that could run apps into something Apple had never explicitly made before: a dedicated handheld gaming device.

overview.heading: The fastest iPod touch ever made.
paragraphs: The third-generation iPod touch was announced September 9, 2009 at Apple's "It's Only Rock and Roll" music event — the same event that introduced iTunes 9 and refreshed the iPod lineup. In a break from the iPhone-centric framing of previous iPod touch launches, Apple positioned the 3G almost entirely around gaming, benchmarking it against the Nintendo DS and PlayStation Portable.

Inside the unchanged aluminum and stainless steel chassis sat hardware borrowed directly from the iPhone 3GS: a Samsung ARMv7 Cortex-A8 core clocked at 600 MHz, the PowerVR SGX535 GPU with OpenGL ES 2.0 support, and 256 MB of RAM — double the 2nd generation's ceiling. Apple called it "50% faster." In practice the gap was wider, particularly in 3D games where the SGX535's shader pipeline ran circles around the older MBX Lite.

The storage lineup contracted sharply. Gone was the 8 GB entry tier and the 16 GB mid-tier. The 3rd generation shipped in 32 GB and 64 GB only — the latter the largest iPod touch Apple had ever shipped. Pricing held at $299 and $399.
One notable first: the 3rd generation was the first iPod touch to ship with earbuds that included a remote and microphone, enabling Voice Control — a feature previously exclusive to iPhone 3GS.

What Apple did not announce was a camera. Pre-release leaks, third-party case packaging at Best Buy, and a subsequent iFixit teardown all told the same story: the 3rd generation was designed to include a rear camera, the socket was physically present inside the device, and something — a manufacturing problem, a cost decision, or a strategic choice — removed it at the last moment. Apple said nothing.

iOS support extended to iOS 5.1.1, released May 2012 — nearly three years of updates. The device could not run iOS 6, which required ARMv7 features the 3G's SoC technically met but Apple chose not to support.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (4th generation)
hero.desc: The fourth generation iPod touch was the device that finally made people believe the iPod touch mattered. A Retina display sharp enough to embarrass every screen around it. Cameras — both front and rear — for the first time in the line's history. FaceTime without a phone plan. It was the iPhone 4's closest cousin, and for millions of people who couldn't afford or didn't want a carrier contract, it was the better deal.

overview.heading: The iPhone 4, without the phone.
paragraphs: The fourth-generation iPod touch was announced September 1, 2010 at Apple's annual iPod event and released twelve days later. It arrived in the same season as the iPhone 4, and Apple made no secret of the relationship — the two devices shared the same Apple A4 processor, the same Retina display at 960×640 and 326 PPI, the same FaceTime capability, and a form factor that was, at 7.2 mm, actually thinner than the iPhone 4.

The headline features were the cameras. For the first time in the iPod touch's history, the device had both a front-facing FaceTime camera and a rear-facing iSight camera capable of 720p video. FaceTime over Wi-Fi — Apple's video calling system, introduced months earlier with the iPhone 4 — was now available to anyone, without a phone plan or a carrier contract. For schools, for children, for anyone who wanted a connected device without a monthly bill, this was the entry point.

The Retina display was the other watershed moment. The jump from the 3G's 163 PPI to 326 PPI was not incremental — it was a step change visible to the naked eye from the first glance. Text sharpened. Photos clarified. Games rendered at a pixel density that, in 2010, had no competition.

The hardware story had complications. The A4 chip ran at 800 MHz, faster than the 3G's 600 MHz, but the RAM stayed at 256 MB — half the 512 MB Apple put in the iPhone 4. The rear camera, despite producing 720p video, captured stills at only 0.7 megapixels — a figure that drew immediate criticism given the iPhone 4's 5 MP camera sat in the same device family.

The 4th generation had the longest sales lifespan of any iPod touch to that point: nearly three years, across multiple price drops and a mid-cycle expansion of the SKU lineup. It was discontinued in two phases — the 8 and 64 GB models in October 2012, the 16 and 32 GB models in May 2013 — and its final software update, iOS 6.1.6, arrived in February 2014.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (5th generation)
hero.desc: The fifth generation iPod touch arrived in six colors, with a 5 MP camera, Siri, a 4-inch Retina display, and a playful pop-out wrist loop. It was faster, thinner, more capable, and more colorful than anything before it in the line — and it arrived the same day as the iPhone 5, sharing its design language without its price. For millions of people who wanted an iPhone but not a contract, the 5G was the answer.

overview.heading: The iPhone 5's closest relative — and the most colorful iPod ever made.
paragraphs: The fifth generation iPod touch was announced on September 12, 2012 alongside the iPhone 5 and went on sale October 11. It was a sweeping redesign: the display grew from 3.5 to 4 inches, the resolution moved to 1136×640 in a 16:9 aspect ratio, the rear camera jumped from 0.7 megapixels to 5 megapixels with an LED flash and 1080p video, and the processor moved from the single-core A4 to the dual-core A5 — doubling RAM from 256 MB to 512 MB in the process. The 30-pin dock connector was replaced with Lightning.

The headline, though, was color. Apple offered the 5th generation in Slate, Silver, Pink, Yellow, and Blue at launch — a range of options the iPod touch had never had. Each color came with a matching wrist loop, attached via a pop-out button on the lower-left of the back. A PRODUCT(RED) variant followed in November 2012, completing what became the most distinctive iPod touch lineup in the line's history.

Siri arrived on the iPod touch for the first time. Previously restricted to the iPhone 4S and later the iPad, Apple's voice assistant now worked on a device without a phone plan. Combined with the 5 MP camera, the 4-inch screen, and the A5's significantly improved graphics performance, the 5G was the first iPod touch that genuinely felt like a peer to the current iPhone rather than a generation behind.

The 5G's history is complicated by a budget variant. In May 2013, Apple quietly introduced a 16 GB model (A1509) that stripped out the rear camera, the LED flash, the wrist loop attachment, and all non-Silver colors — at $229. This model existed to fill the entry price point left by the discontinued 4th generation. It drew immediate criticism. In June 2014, Apple replaced it with a proper 16 GB A1421 model that restored the camera and all six colors at body_class: wiki-page wiki-apple 99.

The 5th generation was discontinued on July 14, 2015 with the announcement of the 6th generation. Its final software update, iOS 9.3.5, arrived August 25, 2016 — a security patch for a critical vulnerability in older 32-bit devices. iOS 10 excluded the 5G entirely, citing its 32-bit A5 processor.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (6th generation)
hero.desc: After two and a half years of silence, the sixth generation iPod touch arrived with the Apple A8 — the same chip as the iPhone 6 — an 8 MP camera, 1 GB of RAM, and a fresh palette topped by a new gold finish. The chassis was the thinnest Apple had ever shipped at 6.1 mm, externally near-identical to the 5G except for one thing: the pop-out Loop button was gone. It was the biggest internal leap in the line's history wrapped in the most familiar body.

overview.heading: The longest wait in the line — answered with the iPhone 6's brain.
paragraphs: The sixth generation iPod touch was released through the online Apple Store on July 15, 2015, alongside refreshed colors for the iPod nano and iPod shuffle. It was the first major update to the iPod touch in more than two and a half years — the 5th generation had launched in September 2012 — and Apple framed it as "the best iPod touch yet." Manufactured by Foxconn, it carried the model number A1574 and the firmware identifier iPod7,1.

The headline was the processor. The 6G adopted the 64-bit Apple A8 — the same system-on-chip as the iPhone 6 and 6 Plus, the iPad mini 4, and later the Apple TV HD and HomePod — paired with the M8 motion coprocessor. RAM doubled from 512 MB to 1 GB of LPDDR3. The rear camera jumped from 5 MP to an 8 MP iSight with 1080p video, and Wi-Fi gained 802.11ac support. For the first time, the iPod touch shipped with the current iPhone's processor rather than a hand-me-down a generation or two behind.

The color story expanded. The 6G launched in space gray, silver, gold, pink, blue, and (PRODUCT)RED. Gold was new to the line, mirroring the iPhone's 2013 expansion. The space gray model had a black glass front; the other five had white fronts. The aluminum unibody was retained, but the pop-out Loop button — the signature flourish of the 5G — was quietly removed, leaving the only visible external difference between the two generations.

Storage was the most generous the line had ever offered: 16, 32, 64, and 128 GB, priced at body_class: wiki-page wiki-apple 99, $249, $299, and $399. The 128 GB tier was a first for any iPod touch. The device shipped with iOS 8.4, released two weeks earlier on June 30, 2015 alongside Apple Music and the Beats 1 radio station — making the 6G one of the launch vehicles for Apple's streaming era.

There was a catch buried in the spec sheet. The A8 in the 6G was underclocked to 1.1 GHz, down from the 1.4 GHz of the iPhone 6, a concession to the smaller battery. The 16 GB base model also drew criticism for being cramped in the iOS 9 era. Still, the device aged remarkably well: it received iOS 9 through 12, was the oldest device to support iOS 10.3, and Apple has continued shipping iOS 12 security updates — the most recent, iOS 12.5.8, arrived in January 2026, more than a decade after launch. It was discontinued in two stages: the 16 and 64 GB tiers on July 27, 2017, and the 32 and 128 GB tiers on May 28, 2019, when the 7th generation arrived.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (7th generation)
hero.desc: Four years after the 6G, the seventh and final iPod touch arrived with the Apple A10 Fusion — the iPhone 7 chip — paired with 2 GB of RAM and a new 256 GB top tier, the largest storage ever offered on an iPod. Externally it was indistinguishable from the 6G it replaced. It added support for Group FaceTime and augmented reality, became one of the launch devices for Apple Arcade, and on May 10, 2022 closed the book on a product line that had run for twenty-one years.

overview.heading: The final iPod — built around the iPhone 7's chip.
paragraphs: The seventh generation iPod touch was released on May 28, 2019, through the online Apple Store. Like the 6G four years earlier, it was a quiet press-release launch rather than a stage moment — but it carried the same model designation lineage, the same Foxconn manufacturing, and a successor's part number: A2178, firmware identifier iPod9,1.

The headline, as in 2015, was the processor. Apple swapped the 6G's A8 for the 64-bit A10 Fusion — the same chip that drove the iPhone 7 and 7 Plus in 2016 — paired with the M10 motion coprocessor. RAM doubled again, to 2 GB of LPDDR4. The PowerVR GT7600 Plus delivered Apple's claim of three times faster graphics. The 7G also became the first iPod to support immersive augmented reality, Group FaceTime, and (later that fall) Apple Arcade — the streaming game service that arrived in September 2019.

The six colors carried over from the 6G unchanged: space gray, silver, gold, pink, blue, and (PRODUCT)RED. The aluminum unibody was identical down to the millimetre — same 6.1 mm depth, same 88 g weight, same 4-inch Retina display at 1136×640. Anyone holding a 6G and a 7G side by side could not distinguish them externally. The only way to tell was to look at the chip identifier in Settings.

Storage tiers were where the 7G made its other real move: 32, 128, and 256 GB at $199, $299, and $399. The 256 GB option was new — the largest capacity any iPod had ever offered, and a deliberate appeal to music libraries kept locally rather than streamed. The device shipped with iOS 12.3, released the same day, May 28, 2019.

Three years later, on May 10, 2022, Apple announced the iPod touch would be sold while supplies last. The accompanying press release, titled "The music lives on," framed the discontinuation as a victory rather than an ending: the iPod's role had been fully absorbed into the iPhone, Apple Watch, HomePod, and Apple Music. Stock sold out within days. The 7G was the last iPod ever made — closing a product line that had launched on October 23, 2001 with the original click-wheel model. Apple has continued shipping iOS 15 security updates: the most recent, iOS 15.8.7, arrived on March 11, 2026.
